title: Emergency Patch: Keeping Change Under Control
context: A critical vulnerability is announced on an application server. The business demands an immediate patch before next week's CAB meeting.

n1.text: The business lead asks to apply the patch tonight without going through the CAB. What do you do first?

choices.text: Open an emergency ticket, assign an owner, and analyze the impact before any decision
choices.why: Even when urgent, a change remains tracked: owner, scope, and impact must be established.

choices.text: Apply the patch immediately to save time
choices.why: Without impact analysis or approval, the patch itself can become the cause of an incident.

choices.text: Wait for next week's CAB without doing anything
choices.why: Leaving a critical vulnerability open is risky; emergency change procedures exist for this.

n2.text: The analysis reveals that the server depends on a legacy application and rebooting will interrupt a business service. What preparation is essential?

choices.text: Schedule a maintenance window, notify stakeholders, and prepare a tested backout plan
choices.why: Dependencies, downtime, maintenance window, and backout plan are the key elements of a complete change request.

choices.text: Reboot without warning: the downtime will only be a few minutes
choices.why: An unannounced outage on a legacy application can have a major business impact.

choices.text: Modify allow lists to work around the issue and avoid rebooting
choices.why: Broadening an allow list weakens security and must be analyzed, not improvised.

n3.text: The patch is applied, but authentication fails. What is the best decision?

choices.text: Execute the backout within the window, document the failure, and resubmit the request to the CAB
choices.why: The backout plan exists for this scenario; the failure should inform a new analysis.

choices.text: Disable MFA to restore access quickly
choices.why: Removing a security control under pressure increases risk.

choices.text: Close the ticket and wait for the next patch cycle
choices.why: A failed change must be documented and re-analyzed, never closed as successful.

n4.outcome: You maintained change traceability, analyzed dependencies, and used the backout plan as intended.

debrief: An emergency does not eliminate the process: ticket, owner, impact analysis, and approval remain necessary.
A maintenance window, announced downtime, and a tested backout plan protect both the business and security.
A failure is documented and returned to the CAB; it is never masked by weakening controls.
